title: LTI analysis of RC and RLC circuits

sections.heading: The idea
sections.body_md:
Circuits built from resistors, capacitors and inductors are LTI systems. Each element law is linear: \(v = iR\), \(i = C\,dv/dt\), \(v = L\,di/dt\). Combining them with Kirchhoff's laws gives a linear differential equation with constant coefficients, so all the LTI tools apply.

A series RC driven by a source is first order, with time constant \(\tau = RC\). A series RLC is second order, with natural frequency \(\omega_0 = 1/\sqrt{LC}\) and damping set by the resistance. To find \(\tau\) in a larger first-order circuit, turn off the independent sources and find the resistance seen by the capacitor.

Initial conditions come from continuity: a capacitor's voltage and an inductor's current cannot jump. After a switch event, the circuit moves exponentially from that starting value to its new DC steady state, where capacitors are open and inductors are short.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body_md: A 47 kΩ resistor charges a 330 nF capacitor from a 9 V source. Then \(\tau = 15.5\ \mathrm{ms}\), the voltage reaches 5.7 V after one time constant, and it is within 1% of 9 V after 78 ms. Adding a 0.2 H inductor in series gives \(\omega_0 = 3890\ \mathrm{rad/s}\) and \(\zeta \approx 30\), heavily overdamped.

sections.heading: Common pitfalls
sections.body_md:
- Using the source resistance alone instead of the Thevenin resistance.
- Letting a capacitor voltage jump at a switch.
- Confusing \(\omega_0\) in rad/s with hertz.

sections.heading: Where this leads
sections.body_md: Replacing the differential equation by impedances leads to circuit transfer functions and frequency response.
